Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

vignette:
Ravi was twenty-six when the relationship that had felt like a rescue became the thing he needed rescuing from. He had been with Priya for just over a year, living together in the apartment above his small convenience store in Jackson Heights. What started as sharp words during arguments escalated slowly-a shove, a slap, then the night she pinned him against the bathroom wall, her forearm across his throat, her body slick with sweat from the summer heat. He remembered the smell most clearly: the sour salt of her skin mixed with the floral air freshener, the way it filled his nose even as his vision went spotty. He did not fight back. He told himself later that he had frozen, that he had not believed it was really happening, that if he just stayed still she would stop. She did stop, eventually. But in the months that followed, Ravi could not stop replaying that moment of paralysis, and the guilt that came with it hardened into something immovable: he would never forgive himself for not doing more.

The sweat smell began appearing everywhere. A customer would walk past him in the store, and Ravi would catch a whiff of body odor and feel his chest lock, the memory of that bathroom wall crashing over him without warning. Sometimes he felt the full emotional intensity of the event-the rage, the shame, the terror-without any clear image surfacing at all, just a wave of heat and hatred that left him gripping the counter. Certain conversation topics became landmines: anyone discussing arguments, relationships, or power dynamics made his throat tighten and his jaw clench, and he would excuse himself to the stockroom, where he stood breathing through his nose until the feeling passed. He had come to believe that his body was the problem-that it kept reacting as if he were still pinned against that wall, even when he was perfectly safe. Living at that pitch of alertness, the world had become dense with reminders he couldn't stop reading-a customer's raised voice, a door slamming, even the scent of floral air freshener suddenly felt like a message, each one confirming what his body already believed. And if he could not trust his own body, how could he trust himself? He began to see himself as fundamentally unreliable, someone who could not be counted on to act when it mattered. That belief colored everything: every stranger who approached him in the store was a potential threat, especially after dusk, when the streetlights cast long shadows and the store felt too quiet. He started closing early, losing regular customers. His girlfriend, Maya, noticed he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind, and she stopped doing it, which only made him feel more alone.

The loop tightened without him naming it. A trigger-the smell, a conversation, a sudden memory-would spike his sense of threat, and that hypervigilance made him scan his environment more aggressively, which made him notice more potential triggers. The more he believed he could not rely on himself, the more he watched for danger, and the more danger he saw, the more that belief was confirmed. At night he could not fall asleep without checking the locks three times, and when he did sleep, he woke gasping from dreams he could not remember, the smell of sweat still in his nostrils. His rage on recall frightened him most: sometimes, remembering Priya's face, he would feel a fury so pure and hot that he worried he might become the person she had been. That rage made him avoid the memory, but avoiding it only made the intrusions more sudden, more vivid, more disorienting.

What finally brought Ravi to therapy was not the sleeplessness or the lost revenue, though both had accumulated. It was a Tuesday evening in late autumn, when a man in a heavy coat walked into the store and Ravi caught the faintest trace of body odor. He felt the memory hit him like a physical blow, and before he knew what he was doing, he had grabbed a box cutter from under the counter and was standing behind it, knuckles white, ready to defend himself against a customer who had only wanted a pack of gum. The man left without buying anything, looking confused and a little scared. Ravi stood in the empty store for a long time, the box cutter still in his hand, and thought: I cannot keep living like this. He was afraid of what he might do next. He was afraid of what he had already become. But underneath that fear, there was a quieter, more desperate hope: that somewhere inside him, the person who had frozen against that bathroom wall might still learn how to move.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat leads to or causes triggers; the vignette describes triggers leading to threat, not the reverse.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat leads to or causes triggers; the vignette describes triggers leading to threat, not the reverse.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
